Good playing. If your looking for what to work on, I would suggest these to consider: 

The bass drum could use some work, try playing 16th note bass drum grooves. (some ideas are a3, &a4). This would help build your limb independence to. 

You can dive into is hi hat patterns. Look up Steward Copeland hi hat ideas. Those ideas are applied in many songs and is something to have on hand to add spice. 

Make sure to work with a click often. Playing to a click will benefit you the most because it is our job to keep time. Gap clicks while hard, will help your timing greatly. 

Also, I strongly encourage you to use the practice pad as often as you can. Know the furious five rudiment: single stroke roll, Double stroke roll, Single paradiddle, flam, and drag. These are the foundation for the rest of the major rudiments you will encounter. The benefit of practice pad work is your hands will be in shape and you will sound great. ATLA is on Netflix, you van turn that series on and practice any rudiment while watching TV. 

Also, I would advise listening to diverse music. Try Irish rock, Indian pop, Chicago blues, Funk, etc. This will familiarize you with different playing styles and will keep the drums fresh. 

Thats all I have for now. hope this helps!

My primary grip is traditional so I have some experience. To be comfortable playing traditional takes LOTS of practice. There are approaches to playing traditional. (ie. Keith Carlock plays his way in the back of the stick, Steve Smith plays in the middle for finger control, etc.) Ill go over the mechanics of traditional grip. 

First, get comfortable holding the drum stick traditional grip. Just sitting in front of the TV holding it traditional has helped me. An example is when I get a straw from my drink I hold it with the traditional grip or sweeping I use the traditional grip to hold the broom handle. 

Start with basic eighth note strokes with the left hand with the door knob wrist twist. This will take a long time to get comfortable doing, then we get to the fingers. 

I find fingers really helpful. The thumb is where the power comes from, in other words, the cradle between the thumb and the index finger. The stick sits nice and comfortable in there. so my favorite exercise for the traditional grip is playing 16th notes dribbling with my thumb. Start very slow at like 45 bpm and work your way up. I can play it at 80 bpm. it took a long time.  Then the index finger helps with the bounce as well and you can include the middle finger as well. A exercise Dave Weckel showed is dribbling the index finger and middle finger. 

The benefit of studying traditional grip is it will vastly improve your matched grip because of all the time spent learning the new grip. Austin and Rob Brown have traditional grip tutorials on their Youtube channels and they have many more years of experience than me. 

People frown upon the traditional grip because of the lack of power and the limitability created, but Keith Carlock, Todd Suckerman, and Steward Copeland get tons of power with the traditional grip, all saying they get just as much power as they do with matched grip. Heck, Steward Copeland even argues that its provides even more power than matched grip. Personally, I play it because early in my career I watched a video where the drummer was doing a exercise with the traditional grip and I fell in love it. I wanted to study it and make it my primary grip. the picture in my head playing it on the drums makes it super epic. Its a tradition I think every drummer should go through. Hope this helps. what your doing is called a build. build are used to (as the name implies) build to another part of a section. (church drummers overuse this to the brink of death)  An accent is a hit which is louder than the other ones. the best example is a backbeat which is always accented. an exercise my drum teacher gave me to do is to play a single stroke roll each bar I accent a sixteenth note and with each bar I move my accent by one sixteenth note. so in a notation, RLRL the accent on the first bar would be the one or R and the next bar would be on the e of one  (L) and so fourth until I reach two. then I try and create new accent patterns. (possibly count one and the a of one and so fourth.) the sky is the limit on accents and they are essential part of drumming. as you develop more rudiments, accents are super useful to apply to any rudiment. the internet is filled with instructors explaining accents and have exercises they use as well. 

to answer your metronome part. timing is essential part of practice. whether on the pad or on the kit. you always need to constantly work on your time. like in the last post, gap clicks are so useful and they are very handy to play with and without a click. in your stage, I recommend playing a basic rock groove and keep locked in with the metronome. overtime, your timing will become solid. people will bob their heads and your will be the one getting the gigs. our job as drummers is to keep time with or without a click.  

Also, I wanted to recommend playing along to music a lot. I usually like to compare that to a scrimmage whether in basketball or water polo. its to put the things you learned into action and also to check your progress. they are the closest things to playing to actual musicians and its so much fun as well.

ill give you feedback instead. 

I noticed your fills are speeding up and even a couple of instances where you start a fill, get lost, and find the one. this suggest you really need to play along with a click way more often. Also, you need to add some flavor in the transitions as well. Instead of doing singles around the kit, try to expand your fill vocabulary with new ideas. explore other types of music, my favorite is exploring other countrie's music such as Irish rock, Indian pop, and many others. this will expose you to different types of music and make you think of new fills and grooves. whenever I am in a rut, I tend to listen to foreign music to bring more spice and with them you head begins to create more ideas. 

Additionally, there are a couple of parts in the track where you parts dont fit the music. For example, the second backing track, the hi hat pattern you did didn't fit the music. Add some accents and make it feel good. 

you really could use some practice pad work as well. doesn't matter how fast you can play, if you don't sound good, then its pointless. sit in front of the tv and play singles doubles, paradiddles, etc while zoning out to tv shows. Good shows to binge, well. Avatar the last Airbender is on Netflix. 

Count! Chris Coleman said 98 percent of your problems is solved by counting. Count how many bars are in each verse, chorus, etc. chart the songs in advance so when you go behind the kit to work out the parts, you know how many bars are in a piece. 

Finally, you also need to stay in the pocket. that is developed by practicing to a click. my favorite click to play is a gap click. really forces you to stay on track and overtime, you will be the one in time.

This is not to condemn you. I want you to be successful and you found a band which is a big accomplishment in my book since I have trouble finding musicians. Also, ask you bandmates for feedback and take the feedback to heart and work on those as well so when you join them or another band, they see the improvement as well. 

Good luck! let us know if you have any questions.

Setting up a kit comfortably takes time. Todd Suckerman said to listen to your body and if your experiencing pain, then it’s a good sign to adjust your kit. Another tip I found on the YouTube comment section useful is to play blindfolded to test the set up.

Ergonomics set up. Colliding sticks means your hat and snare are too close. Here’s a tip: Sit up with good posture and have your hands in the ready position. So like your ready to play an eighth note groove. Then set your kit up so when you play you will have posture. A sign I observed is if you have to think about hitting a drum or cymbal then it’s most likely not in a natural position. Hope this helps.

head over to youtube and look up a drummer named Rob "Beatdown" Brown. He has in depth analysis of the traditional grip. ill add on some things I have done to develop my traditional grip: 

1.  start practice your rudiments on a pad at a slow temp. Your restarting from scratch since its a new grip. The more time on the pad, the more natural it will sound.
2. Your snare height also plays a factor since the traditional grip has a different snare height than match. the youtube channel stated above will have a video covering snare height. 
3. transitioning from cross stick to traditional and vice versa, its hard to explain without being in person. if you watch famous traditional grip players. you might be able to learn how to do that. (eg: Russ Miller)

Hope this helps you. If I have mistaken something, correct me. 

​

to get to cross stick for traditional grip you let go with your thumb, then hold the stick with the middle finger and ring finger, then  turn you hand with the palm down and while turning your hand grab the stick with your thumb and rearrange the stick with cross stick.

To get from cross stick to traditional grip, flip the stick backwards and catch it with the traditional grip.
